stories.headline: Ousted Ukraine Def Min urges wartime election, warning of governance crisis
stories.title: Ousted Ukraine Def Min urges wartime election, warning of governance crisis
stories.summary: Ukraine's ousted Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called Tuesday for elections to be held even as the war against Russia continues, saying the country was gripped by a crisis of governance. The move by one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's most loyal and longstanding team members until recently could become the most significant internal challenge Zelenskyy has faced since Russia's full-scale invasion. The appeal came in a video address posted to YouTube by Fedorov, who lost his post in July. "We must find a legal, safe, and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process even amid a prolonged war," Fedorov said. Zelenskyy's office did not immediately comment on Fedorov's address. Ukrainian law prohibits elections while the country is under martial law, which was imposed on Feb. 24, 2022, the day that the Russian invasion began. Fedorov said the country was facing a systemic crisis in how it is governed, arguing the current system is oriented tow

stories.headline: YSRCP urges State Election Commission to defer municipal rolls until SIR completion
stories.title: YSRCP urges State Election Commission to defer municipal rolls until SIR completion
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party (YSRCP) has submitted a representation requesting that the Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission (SEC) conduct elections for Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, and Nagar Panchayats only after the completion of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and the publication of final electoral rolls.

The YSRCP State general secretary Lella Appi Reddy, in the letter, raised concerns over the SEC’s current directive requiring authorities to publish ward-wise photo electoral rolls using January 1, 2026, as the qualifying date.

The YSRCP leader pointed out that draft Assembly electoral rolls published on July 31, 2026, revealed significant discrepancies across all 175 constituencies, placing approximately 42 lakh entries under scrutiny and leading to the deletion of 44.89 lakh entries.
These deletions included roughly 15.22 lakh deceased voters and 7.37 lakh duplicate or multiple registrations, alongside numerous untraceable or shifted individuals.
He claimed that issuing ward-wise municipal rolls relying on draft electoral data would create serious inconsistencies.

Furthermore, because the claims and objections process under the SIR is ongoing through the statutory framework of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, finalising municipal rolls beforehand risks excluding genuine eligible voters whose applications remain under review.

Citing Section 11 of the Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965, which provides that municipal rolls be derived from updated Assembly rolls, the party requested the SEC to adjust its schedule to align with the final SIR roll publication, he added.

stories.headline: Border Defines India: But who defines border citizen?
stories.title: Border Defines India: But who defines border citizen?
stories.summary: As the 80 th anniversary of Independence Day dawns, the country will simply go into an overdrive with customary grandeur. The Tricolour will flutter atop important buildings; schoolchildren will sing patriotic songs, and speeches will extol the sacrifices that won us freedom from our colonial masters. A nation- state is defined by two of its very distinct facets—its people who populate its entire length and breadth and off course the national boundaries/borders. Both of these entities find ample space and discourse in its constitution and are complementary to each other. Not one of them individually can define the concept of a nation-state on its own steam. No wonder eighty years back, when Cyril Radcliffe the British lawyer cum boundary commission chairman set out his task of defining the national boundaries of India and Pakistan in a mere forty five days span , even he wouldn’t have realized the importance of carving out such a ‘cartographic lineation’. Since this lineation was followed by one of the biggest human displacements with bloody repercussions in modern times across the Radcliffe line, hence the uniqueness of this partition.The borders of a country are not merely ‘cartographic labyrinthine’ but a place where the republic is tested every single day. It is where the idea of India ceases to be an abstraction and becomes a lived reality. Ironically, while the border defines India’s geography, the ‘border citizen’ often remains invisible in India’s policymaking. For close to seventy nine years, India has viewed its national borders primarily through the prism of military strategy, investing in troops, weapons, surveillance and other infra to protect its territorial integrity. These investments are indispensible no doubt, but they also reveal a deeper flaw in our national thinking right from 1947. We have treated borders as military spaces to be defended rather than living spaces to be nurtured. This distinction matters, and hence my endeavour to pen down this write up on India’s 80 th Independence day to put under the scanner such a distinction which may not portend well for our country if left untreated. A nation-state is not merely secured by its armed forces guarding its borders. It is secured when citizens choose to live there with dignity, confidence and hope. Every inhabited village on the border is a declaration of national sovereignty. Every family that refuses to abandon its ancestral home despite enemy shelling, infiltration or isolation is performing an act of national service that rarely finds mention from the ramparts of Red fort of India. Nowhere is this reality more visible than in Jammu & Kashmir. Border residents have lived through wars since 1947, terrorist violence, repeated ceasefire violations and prolonged uncertainty. Children have grown up distinguishing mortar fire from festival fireworks, farmers have cultivated fields under the shadow of sniper fire and many more such vagaries as thrown up by our inimical western neighbour at us. These are not isolated tragedies. But represent a way of life that few Indians living hundreds of Kilometers away can fully comprehend. Out of a stated fifteen thousand kilometers of total land boundary of India touching seven neighbouring nations, how much of border is actually under fire of ours? I may dare say only that which abuts our western neighbour in the UT of J&K and now under an uneasy calm punctuated by repeated ceasefire violations. Isn’t it suitable time on the anvil of 80 th Independence Day of India, that these hapless people are not left to the mercy of geo-political machinations of this sub-continent which are played with utter disregard to their wellbeing? Be that as it may, yet public policy frequently views border districts through the lens of relief rather than resilience. Compensation is announced after damage, roads are sanctioned after strategic necessity arises. Same is the case with a plethora of welfare schemes involving schools, hospitals and employment opportunities. In the after math of mayhem unleashed by Pakistan last year during ‘Op Sindoor’ on our border villages abutting both the IB and the LC, stories of continued neglect, administrative cum bureaucratic apathy emanate from media circles regarding laggardly pace of redevelopment of damaged infra. Leave alone relief, resilience is a far cry for us to come on top of the things as they stand today. The contrast with China is instructive. Both India & China threw out the yolk of slavery in the late 1940s. With a gap of only two years in between i.e. 1947 and 1949 respectively, China has pursued an integrated border strategy in which civilian settlements, economic development and military preparedness reinforce each other thereby surpassing India both in thought and action. Many of the readers of my article may argue that being a totalitarian cum communist nation, for China the concept of a nation-state supersedes its denizens. This is passé, simple and straight. For the sake of argument even if I do take this concept as viable, then may I ask why India has woken up lately to emulate the same concept in the format of VVP (Vibrant village programme now? The villages of China all along the LAC in our context present themselves the ‘Chinese instrument of national security, signaling that the writ of mandarins of power in Beijing runs not only in their national capital but right till the last village of theirs. Though India as stated above has lately started in the right earnest to rectify decades of its inertia in such matters, by kicking starting programmes like the VVP it is too late and too less. The intent though commendable, the scheme doesn’t inspire that much confidence. As late as a few weeks back, the PM in one of his discourses with the youth of India under the aegis of DIYLD (Developed India Young Leaders’ Dialogue) presented an idea before them of visiting border villages, staying, and connecting with them instead of using the virtual media to do so. This suggestion by our honourable PM throws an interesting question instead—‘Is merely encouraging the youth of India to visit these border villages enough? Can these cosmetics change the dismal situation as found present in these frontier areas? I shall not dwell much upon this topic, since it is being tackled by me in a separate article from Rising Kashmir paper. Border citizens per se ought to be placed head and shoulders above the rest of the populace of our country. Their defining attributes being derived from their very stay in the border areas and acting as the sentinels of a democratic dispensation in a region surrounded by theocratic countries. As India enters its eightieth year of independence, perhaps the time is ripe enough to redefine the citizenry of our border areas who, away from the din of the mainstream living of India, are silently carving out an existence for themselves based on true values of nationalism. The strength of a nation cannot be measured in terms of its military or economic might. But from the confidence of its citizens living at its farthest edge. If the border defines India’s territorial identity, then the ‘border citizens’ define its moral identity. How India treats those who stand at its frontiers reveals what kind of republic it truly is. (The author is a retired army officer and a regular scribe of Rising Kashmir. He can be approached at his email: slalotra4729@gmail.com)

stories.headline: Supreme Court 9-Judge Bench To Pronounce Judgment Tomorrow On Correctness Of 'Industry' Definition
stories.title: Supreme Court 9-Judge Bench To Pronounce Judgment Tomorrow On Correctness Of 'Industry' Definition
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court will tomorrow pronounce its judgment on reconsideration of the expansive definition of "industry" given in Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board.
A. Rajappa (1978).

A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and comprising Justices BV Nagarathna, PS Narasimha, Dipankar Datta, Ujjal Bhuyan, Satish Chandra Sharma, Joymalya Bagchi, Alok Aradhe and Vipul M Pancholi heard on the limited issue of whether the Bangalore Water Supply judgment was rightly decided and reserved for judgment on March 19.
The Constitution Bench was examining whether the broad interpretation of “industry” adopted in the 1978 judgment authored by Justice VR Krishna Iyer requires reconsideration.
In the Bangalore Water Supply case, a seven-judge bench had laid down a sweeping interpretation of the term “industry” under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

The Court held that any systematic activity organised by cooperation between employer and employee for the production or distribution of goods and services could fall within the definition of industry, even if the organisation was not engaged in profit-making.

(i) Whether the test laid down in paragraphs 140 to 144 in the opinion rendered by Hon'ble Mr. Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer in Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board's case (supra) to determine if an undertaking or enterprise falls within the definition of “industry” lays down correct law?

And whether the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1982 (which seemingly did not come into force) and the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (with effect from 21.11.2025) have any legal impact on the interpretation of the expression “industry” as contained in the principal Act?

(ii) Whether social welfare activities and schemes or other enterprises undertaken by the Government Departments or their instrumentalities can be construed to be “industrial activities” for the purpose of Section 2(j) of the ID Act?
(iii) What State activities will be covered by the expression “sovereign function”, and whether such activities will fall outside the purview of Section 2(j) of the ID Act?
The reference arises out of a 2002 appeal.
In 2005, a five-judge bench, headed by Justice N.Santosh Hegde, referred the Bangalore Water supply case to a larger bench, in State of Uttar Pradaesh.

stories.headline: Union cabinet approves quadrupling of Gummidipoondi-Gudur section
stories.title: Union cabinet approves quadrupling of Gummidipoondi-Gudur section
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'cabinet approves' in title weight 44
candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: The Central government has sanctioned ₹2,229 crore for the construction of the third and fourth lines from Gummidipoondi to Gudur.
The decision was taken at a Union Cabinet meeting held in New Delhi on Wednesday.
According to a press release, the quadrupling of the tracks from Gummidipoondi to Gudur was announced along with four other railway projects in the country with a total outlay of ₹13,000-crore.

The Gummidipoondi – Gudur section, at present, has double lines and forms part of both the New Delhi to Chennai and Howrah to Chennai high density network routes, so it has been decided to construct third and fourth lines.
The section also falls under the Vizag–Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC) and forms part of the planned East Coast Economic Corridor (ECEC), which is the country’s first coastal corridor.

stories.headline: Supreme Court turns to Gen Z, Gen Alpha to educate elders on solid waste management
stories.title: Supreme Court turns to Gen Z, Gen Alpha to educate elders on solid waste management
stories.summary: The Court questions the notion that waste is a problem of the sanitary workers alone; says every individual should take responsibility and asks District Collectors to engage with households and educational institutions
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: A concerned Supreme Court has turned to Gen Z and Gen Alpha to “educate” their elders against the careless and excessive generation of everyday garbage, saying a miniscule number of sanitary workers across the country cannot be expected to deal with solid waste produced by a population of 1.4 billion.

A Bench headed by Justice S.V.N. Bhatti said the “general feeling” across society was regrettably that ‘I am entitled to generate but not to cooperate and control the impact of solid waste management at the threshold’.

“The prevailing assumption that solid waste is a problem for sanitary workers alone, while the rest of the population remains passive generators, is neither legally correct nor practically sustainable, and is constitutionally unethical,” the top court said in an order passed on August 18, but released on Wednesday (August 19, 2026).
Continued complacency would lead to pandemic and endemic situations, the court warned.

“The volume and complexity of solid waste, i.e., biodegradable, non-biodegradable, hazardous, electronic and construction, have outgrown what any single class of workers can be expected to absorb or handle.
The infrastructure needs a complete audit and upgradation to meet the extant standards of the Solid Waste Management (SWM) Rules, 2026,” the court said.

In fact, the imbalance between the volume of the solid waste being generated and the infrastructure to collect it had so alarmed the Supreme Court on May 25 that it constituted a committee of five Union Secretaries of the Ministries of Housing and Urban Affairs; Environment, Forest and Climate Change; Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti; and Panchayati Raj and Rural Development, along with the Member-Secretary of the Central Pollution Control Board, to monitor the situation on a pan-India basis.
But the Bench accepted the reality that law alone cannot induce good civic behaviour.
That had to come from within.

The court agreed with Additional Solicitor-General Aishwarya Bhati that to prevent an environmental disaster, every stakeholder had to cooperate, and the true power to implement the SWM Rules lay with the householders, local body officers and every direct and indirect contributor of solid waste.

In this context, the court referred to how Rule 4 of the Solid Waste Management (SWM) Rules, 2026, casts the duty of segregation, safe storage and handover on the ‘waste generator’, which means every individual, household, institution and establishment.
“Indefinite, exclusive reliance on state supervision of a constitutionally literate citizenry would defeat the object of the Rules,” the Supreme Court said.

The court agreed with Additional Solicitor-General Aishwarya Bhati that to prevent an environmental disaster, every stakeholder had to cooperate, and the true power to implement the SWM Rules lay with the householders, local body officers and every direct and indirect contributor of solid waste.

sentences.text: “The prevailing assumption that solid waste is a problem for sanitary workers alone, while the rest of the population remains passive generators, is neither legally correct nor practically sustainable, and is constitutionally unethical,” the top court said in an order passed on August 18, but released on Wednesday (August 19, 2026).

In fact, the imbalance between the volume of the solid waste being generated and the infrastructure to collect it had so alarmed the Supreme Court on May 25 that it constituted a committee of five Union Secretaries of the Ministries of Housing and Urban Affairs; Environment, Forest and Climate Change; Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti; and Panchayati Raj and Rural Development, along with the Member-Secretary of the Central Pollution Control Board, to monitor the situation on a pan-India basis.

A concerned Supreme Court has turned to Gen Z and Gen Alpha to “educate” their elders against the careless and excessive generation of everyday garbage, saying a miniscule number of sanitary workers across the country cannot be expected to deal with solid waste produced by a population of 1.4 billion.

stories.headline: The Drying Tears of the Himalayas: Why Kashmir’s Water Crisis is a Warning to the World
stories.title: The Drying Tears of the Himalayas: Why Kashmir’s Water Crisis is a Warning to the World
stories.summary: There was a time when summer in Kashmir arrived not as a season, but as a celebration. The gentle snowmelt would breathe life into the Valley, filling the rivers with a rush of crystal-clear water, while the mighty glaciers stood resilient, promising a steady bounty to sustain the land through the sunlit months. Today, that rhythm is broken. Summers now pass in an anxious blur of unprecedented heatwaves and parched earth, reducing once-roaring streams to a trickle, and the vast water towers of Asia are quietly fading. It is because, in the Paradise on Earth, we are choking the very natural systems meant to protect our future. The Vanishing Mirrors of the Valley The tragedy of Kashmir’s water is unfolding right before our eyes, but it is moving slowly enough that we risk becoming numb to it. According to a new report published on 30, April 2026, “A damning report by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) laid bare a terrifying reality: nearly three out of four lakes in Jammu and Kashmir have either entirely vanished or shrunk dramatically. Out of 697 lakes catalogued across Jammu and Kashmir, 518 have either vanished entirely or shrunk to a shadow of their former selves. These water bodies have been swallowed by reckless urban expansion, concrete encroachments, siltation, pollution and decades of institutional indifference. That is 74 per cent of a region’s liquid heritage, lost. Of the 697 lakes surveyed, 315, nearly 45 per cent, have not just been reduced or degraded but erased completely. One of the major reasons, the CAG’s findings revealed, is a troubling absence of coordination. The Forest Department, Revenue Department, Agriculture Department, Fisheries Department, and the Department of Ecology, Environment and Remote Sensing all hold overlapping mandates. Yet the audit found no unified framework binding them together. Lakes fell through the cracks, not because no one owned them, but because too many agencies did. None was willing to take primary responsibility for their decline. Iconic lifelines like the Dal and Wular lakes, which once acted as massive natural sponges, soaking up excess water to prevent catastrophic floods, are suffocating under layers of untreated sewage and silt. When we destroy a wetland, we don't just lose a view; we destroy nature’s own engineering system for climate resilience. The Melting Lifelines Glaciers in Kashmir act as natural water reservoirs, gradually releasing meltwater into rivers and streams during the summer months. Their continued shrinkage affects irrigation, drinking water supplies, hydropower generation and horticulture-dependent livelihoods across the Valley. The Jhelum river system and several of its tributaries depend heavily on snow and glacier melt originating in the higher Himalayas. Environmentalists say a major and worrying sign is the rapid melting of the glaciers that feed Kashmir’s rivers and streams during summer months. Studies and recent observations have shown accelerated ice loss in several glaciers, including the famous Thajwas Glacier near Sonamarg. Researchers have warned that the glacier has lost a substantial portion of its ice volume over recent decades due to rising temperatures and erratic snowfall patterns. Scientists say glaciers initially release more water as they melt rapidly, but over time the shrinking ice reserves reduce long-term water availability downstream. This threatens irrigation, hydropower generation and drinking water supply for thousands of households dependent on glacier-fed systems. Independent weather observers say Kashmir’s changing climate pattern is becoming increasingly visible through shorter winters, weak western disturbances and prolonged dry spells. If the valleys are losing their mirrors, the mountains are losing their crowns. Kashmir’s glaciers, which have sustained agriculture, orchards, and households for centuries, are retreating at an unprecedented pace. Researchers caution that while accelerated melting may initially increase river flows, the long-term impact could be a decline in water availability as glacier reserves continue to diminish. A report published in National Herald India on 31 May 2026 cites a recent comprehensive study by the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Kashmir, led by noted glaciologist Professor Shakil Ahmad Romshoo (Vice Chancellor, IUST). They analysed nine benchmark glaciers across the Kashmir Himalayas using Landsat satellite data collected between 1980 and 2013. The findings point to a significant climatic shift in the upper reaches of the Valley, where temperatures are rising more rapidly at elevations above 3,000 metres. The study revealed that glaciers in the region have lost nearly 17% of their total area over the past three decades. Even more concerningly, the high Himalayas are warming faster than the low-lying cities. A Global Crisis Hits Home According to meteorological data, Jammu and Kashmir recorded a rainfall deficit of 26 % between March 1 and May 6 this year. The UT also witnessed its seventh consecutive dry winter, with precipitation during December 2025 to February 2026 remaining far below normal. An ETV Bharat news report published on 13 May 2026 highlights that the rainfall shortage has affected districts unevenly, but some areas have recorded alarming deficits. Shopian reported nearly 71 % below-normal rainfall during March-May, making it one of the worst-hit districts. Kathua recorded around 63 % deficiency, followed by Kulgam at 53 %, Anantnag at 46 % and Budgam at 40 %. Kishtwar, Udhampur, Doda, Pulwama, Bandipora and Ramban also remained below seasonal averages. Srinagar recorded a deficit of over 20 % during the same period. If the valleys are losing their mirrors, the mountains are losing their crowns. Kashmir’s glaciers, which have sustained agriculture, orchards, and households for centuries, are retreating at an unprecedented pace. This is no longer a distant threat confined to scientific journals. It is an immediate crisis of water scarcity. According to local meteorological data, Kashmir suffered an alarming rainfall deficit of 26% between March and May this year, hot on the heels of its seventh consecutive dry winter. In districts like Shopian, the deficit skyrocketed to 71%. A recent report by The Guardian highlighted that famous Kolahoi Glacier near Pahalgam is thinning rapidly, losing about 0.65 meters of ice thickness annually for every 1 o C temperature rise. Local farmers in Pulwama and Budgam are already facing the consequences. Irrigation canals that used to flow steadily through the summer are running dry by June. Paddy fields are cracking, and apple orchardists are looking at the sky in despair. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) has consistently warned that mountain ecosystems are the first responders to climate change. When the "Water Towers of Asia" fail, the shockwaves will travel far downstream, threatening the drinking water and food security of millions of people across the subcontinent. Moreover If a region historically defined by its glacial abundance, sprawling wetlands, and endless freshwater can face dry taps, cracked fields, and vanishing springs in 2026, no region on Earth is safe. Kashmir is the canary in the coal mine for global climate resilience. So there is a wake-up call asking us to stop trying to conquer nature with concrete and instead design our future in harmony with it. If we protect nature today, nature will protect us tomorrow. If we allow Kashmir’s glaciers to melt away and its water bodies to turn into dust, we aren't just losing our heritage; we are compromising our very survival. Therefore, let the drying springs of Kashmir be the wake-up call we can no longer afford to ignore. (The author works as a Science Teacher in the J&K School Education Department and is currently Pursuing Research at the School of Education, Central University of Kashmir)

stories.headline: PDP's Iltija demands crop insurance, better infra for apple growers, holds sit-in
stories.title: PDP's Iltija demands crop insurance, better infra for apple growers, holds sit-in
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 19: PDP leader Iltija Mufti on Wednesday held a sit-in protest at a mandi in south Kashmir's Anantnag district in support of crop insurance and better infrastructure for apple growers in Kashmir, saying farmers deserve protection from the losses. Speaking to reporters at the protest site, Jablipora fruit mandi, she said apple growers face losses every year due to the Srinagar-Jammu national highway closure and natural calamities. "Their demands are not like they are out of this world...For example, a crop insurance scheme should be introduced for them because every year we see, whether it is due to road closures, hailstorms, floods, or natural calamities, our apple farmers here in the whole of Jammu and Kashmir, especially in Kashmir, suffer a lot of damage," she said. The PDP leader said the government should waive off their loans and provide better storage facilities and improve transportation facilities. Mufti asserted that horticulture is very important for the economy of Jammu and Kashmir, which kept the economy of the region afloat even during the militancy era. "We know that for so many years, whenever there was a disturbance here, even during the era of militancy, the one thing that kept the economy of Jammu and Kashmir going was horticulture. Charging that the NC government is not paying attention to the farmers' demands, she asserted that her party would not allow the government to favour some capitalists. "If you want to help Adani, you are putting pressure on the Kashmiri apple, our farmers. We will not let this happen. So, to favour some capitalists, you want the fruit economy of Kashmir to shut down; this is completely wrong," she added.
